record.paper_title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
record.context_brief: Q2D conductivity with lattice and pressure
record.original_question: How should one construct a theoretical conductivity model for quasi-two-dimensional organic conductors based on BEDT-TTF (ET) salts that includes as many real material parameters as possible, explicitly incorporates the crystal lattice, and can therefore be used to analyze how high external pressure affects conductivity? The paper frames this as a natural next step given the large body of conductivity measurements on Q2D salts and the expectation that doping changes the chemical potential and thereby influences transport.

evidence.quote: With all the avaliable experimental data on the conductivity of Q2D salts, it is tempting to undertake a theoretical study of the problem, taking into account the influence of as many as possible real material parameters.

It is particularly interesting to try to take into account in this calculation the existence of a crystal lattice, as this gives the possibility to analyze the influence of high external pressure on the conductivity.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider quasi-two-dimensional (Q2D) organic charge-transfer salts based on the donor molecule BEDT-TTF (commonly denoted ET), whose crystal structure consists of weakly coupled conducting layers of ET molecules separated by anion layers. The single-particle electronic structure near the Fermi level is dominated by the highest occupied molecular orbitals of the ET dimers, giving rise to a quarter- or half-filled (depending on the salt) tight-binding band on an anisotropic two-dimensional lattice (typically of κ-, β-, θ- or α-type), with weak interlayer hopping t_⊥ ≪ t_∥. External hydrostatic pressure modifies the intermolecular distances and hence the transfer integrals t_ij and the on-site/intersite Coulomb couplings.

Construct a microscopic theoretical model for the electrical conductivity σ(T, P, μ) of such Q2D ET salts as a function of temperature T, hydrostatic pressure P, and chemical potential μ, satisfying the following requirements:

(i) The model must be defined on the actual three-dimensional crystal lattice of the salt (rather than on a featureless 2D continuum), with transfer integrals {t_ij(P)} and interaction parameters obtained from, or parametrized by, real material data.

(ii) It must incorporate as many physically relevant parameters as possible: the anisotropic intralayer hopping pattern, interlayer hopping, on-site and nearest-neighbor Coulomb interactions, electron–phonon coupling to the relevant lattice modes, and disorder.

(iii) It must give an explicit, pressure-dependent prescription t_ij = t_ij(P), so that σ(T, P, μ) can be computed and compared with measured pressure dependences of the conductivity.

(iv) It must allow the chemical potential μ to vary (modeling doping or band filling) and predict the resulting changes in transport coefficients.

Within this framework, derive a closed expression (or a controlled computational scheme) for the in-plane and out-of-plane conductivity tensor components, and analyze the qualitative and quantitative effect of increasing pressure on σ for representative κ-(ET)_2X salts.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is an open-ended modeling program rather than a precisely posed conjecture. While there is an extensive literature on tight-binding and Hubbard-type models for BEDT-TTF salts (including DFT-parametrized hoppings and pressure-induced changes), no single, universally accepted lattice-based microscopic conductivity theory incorporating all listed material parameters and reproducing the pressure dependence of σ in Q2D ET salts has been established. The problem therefore appears to remain open in its full form.

status_evidence.title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
status_evidence.snippet: Posed as a desirable theoretical next step given available Q2D conductivity data.
status_evidence.claim: Stated as an open program for future theoretical work.
